description: Just some teenagers working on something innovative.
summary:
Far from Earth, astronauts can't wait for a doctor. On the way to Mars, a single message can take up to 22 minutes to reach mission control, so the crew has to notice health problems themselves, often while tired, busy and isolated.

AURA (Astronaut's Urgent Response and Analytics) is a health companion built for that moment. It brings every crew member's vitals and the cabin's air, pressure and radiation into one calm dashboard, then checks each reading three ways: against NASA safety limits, against that astronaut's own normal, and against its trend. That means it can warn "oxygen falling, critical in about 8 minutes" before it happens. Each morning, astronauts log their blood sugar, sleep, mood, stress and how connected they feel. A clickable body map, trend charts and health records help them understand what it means, and every alert explains what to do and when to call the flight surgeon. Because loneliness is a real risk on long missions, AURA also watches wellbeing and makes reaching out easy. An AI assistant explains everything in plain language, and anyone can host their own mission to try it.
details:
What AURA does

On a long mission, nobody is down the hall to check on you. AURA (Astronaut Urgent Response & Analytics) helps astronauts keep an eye on their own health, and each other's, without waiting for Earth.

• One dashboard for the whole crew: heart rate, blood oxygen, blood pressure, breathing and temperature for each astronaut, plus the cabin's CO₂, oxygen, pressure, temperature, humidity and radiation.

• Early warnings, not just alarms: every reading is checked against NASA's safety limits (NASA-STD-3001 for the cabin), against that astronaut's own pre-flight normal, and against its recent trend. So AURA can say "oxygen falling, critical in about 8 minutes" while there is still time to act.

• A one-minute daily check-in: blood sugar, sleep, mood, stress, how connected the astronaut feels, exercise and any symptoms. These are exactly the indicators NASA suggested.

• Clear next steps: every alert says what to do now and when to call the flight surgeon, and is tagged with NASA's five spaceflight hazards and the matching Human Research Program risk.

• A body map: tap the heart, lungs, brain, eyes, blood or bones to see their status, what spaceflight does to them and how to measure them.

• Wellbeing support: loneliness and low mood are real risks on long missions. AURA tracks mood, connection and stress, notices worrying patterns, logs calls home and crew time, and lets an astronaut privately request a talk with the flight psychologist.

• Distance from Earth: live distance, signal delay and how long a return would take, for a space station, the Moon or Mars.

• An AI assistant: answers questions in plain language using the live data, e.g. "Why is my risk level high?" or "What happens in the next hour?"

• Routine and motivation: daily tasks, streaks and a health score keep check-ins a habit.

• History and records: charts over 24 hours to 90 days, a searchable health record for each astronaut, and backup and restore.

• Missions: anyone can host their own mission, like a game server, with its own crew, sensors and scenarios. Training scenarios (hypoxia, fever, a CO₂ scrubber fault, a solar particle event and more) let crews practise spotting problems early.

How it works

Wearables and cabin sensors send readings to AURA's API. Each sensor has its own key, so real hardware (even an ESP32) can plug in without code changes. Until real sensors connect, a built-in simulator generates realistic data. A rule-based analysis engine checks every reading in three ways: against safety limits, against the astronaut's personal baseline, and with a trend forecast. These checks are fully explainable, with no black box deciding whether someone is in danger. The AI assistant only explains the results; it doesn't make the safety decisions.

Benefits and impact

AURA turns raw numbers into understanding and action. It catches slow changes, like a week of poor sleep or growing isolation, as well as fast emergencies. It is designed for crews who are not doctors, which is the situation NASA describes for missions to the Moon and Mars. The same approach could help people in other isolated places, such as Antarctic stations, submarines or remote clinics.

Tools and technologies

• Python (FastAPI) backend and a PostgreSQL database (Supabase)

• React frontend with hand-written CSS

• Google Gemini API for the assistant

• Hosted on Render; everything runs on free tiers

What makes it creative

• It treats the mind as seriously as the body.

• It shows where the crew actually is: how far from Earth and how long help would take.

• Missions let anyone host their own private copy, much like a game server.

• It is designed to feel calm and human rather than like an alarm panel.

What we considered

• Cost: zero; everything runs on free tiers.

• Low computing power: the safety logic is simple rule-based maths rather than heavy AI.

• Accessibility: status uses colour and words, and the app works on phones.

• Privacy and security: missions are isolated from each other, chats are private to each person, admin access needs passwords, every change is recorded in an activity log, and there are rate limits and standard web security protections.

• Honesty: the demo crew and readings are clearly labelled as simulated, and AURA is described as decision support, not a medical device.

Data and resources

NASA Human Research Program pages (Five Hazards, Risks, Ongoing Research), NASA-STD-3001 and NASA OCHMO technical briefs, and CSA resources on radiation and space science.
